av_event.line_text: No, that's, honestly, I think that's a good thing. My dad's a bit like that, he just says it. Saves time.
av_event.what: An elderly cat jumps up onto the grey worktop behind Nicola, walks slowly past the kettle and toaster, and sits down beside the fruit bowl, all in view of the webcam. Nicola doesn't turn round.

text:
A: Hiya, hello, can you hear me okay? Sorry, I've not done one of these before, yeah.
B: Yes, I can hear you. Hi. Erm, I'm Nicola. I think we've only got three minutes, so.
A: Yeah, no, definitely. I'm Daniel. I'm in Newark, so East Midlands. I'm a director at a lettings firm, it's sort of a family business. We manage about a hundred and forty properties round Newark and the villages.
B: Okay. So are you the landlord side or the tenant side?
A: Bit of both, to be honest. Landlords are the clients, but day to day it's mostly tenants ringing me. Boilers, mainly. Had one ring me last Sunday about a boiler, right in the middle of Sunday dinner, you know what I mean. What about yourself?
B: I'm a practice manager at a GP surgery in Basingstoke. So reception, staff, rotas, complaints, the lot. About twelve thousand patients.
A: Oh wow, that's a lot of people. That must be full on.
B: Monday mornings are carnage, to be honest. Phones open at eight and by five past we've got forty people in the queue and everyone's cross with the receptionists. And it's not the receptionists' fault, there just aren't enough appointments. I spend half my morning on the front desk myself.
A: Yeah. No, I can imagine. I sort of get a tiny version of that when it's cold. First frost and everyone's heating packs in at once.
B: Mm.
A: Sorry, I'm not comparing it, obviously yours is a lot more serious.
B: No, it's fine. It's similar in a way. People panic and they want someone to sort it now.
A: Exactly, yeah. I'm quite good with the worried ones, I think, cos I'm a bit of a worrier myself, so.
B: I'm the opposite, I think. Staff say I'm quite blunt. I don't really soften things. If the answer's no, it's no. Erm, I don't know if that's what you're after.
A: No, that's, honestly, I think that's a good thing. My dad's a bit like that, he just says it. Saves time.
B: Sorry, can I ask, did you get told what all this is actually for? I did the puzzle and the photos and nobody's really said.
A: Not really, no. I think it's just sort of how people get on? I wouldn't worry, I'm sure you're doing it right.
B: Right. Okay. I just like to know.
A: Yeah, no, fair. I'm the same. I've got a spreadsheet for every gas safety certificate, colour-coded, so I do get it.
B: Colour-coded. Good. That's what I'd do. We had CQC in a couple of years ago, and honestly, the paperwork side, if it's not written down, it didn't happen. That's what they tell you.
A: That's exactly what they say about deposits. If you've not got the check-in photos, you lose the dispute, every time.
B: There you go then.
A: Do you get much time off, with all that? Do you go away?
B: Cornwall or Devon most summers. And Tenerife, same all-inclusive, I've been three times. I know the hotel's good, so I don't have to worry about it.
A: No way, I've done Tenerife three times as well! Same resort, with the lads. Where were you, south?
B: Costa Adeje.
A: Oh, we were Las Americas, so just down the road, really. It were fine, yeah. I'm a nightmare with flights though. I check in the second it opens.
B: I print the boarding passes as well. Darren, my husband, thinks I'm ridiculous.
A: No, I'd do the same, honestly. Hannah, my girlfriend, laughs at me for it.
B: Well, it's sensible. Things go wrong with phones. Anyway, I think we're probably nearly
